clue.text: Using head after jape, one makes sense

parts.note: an antic is a playful trick or caper
Roman numeral one
pate is an old word for the head

explanation.surface: A practical joker uses their head and finds that the prank makes sense after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The head is placed after the jape and the one, so the order is joke, numeral, head. 'Using' and 'makes' only knit the surface together.
explanation.definitionFit: To anticipate something is to sense or foresee it before it happens, a close synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Force up the pole, breaking off top

indicators.note: in a down answer the top is the first letter, and breaking it off removes it

parts.note: up the pole is British slang for crazy, as is barmy

explanation.surface: Someone forces their way up a flagpole and snaps the top off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up the pole' reads as climbing but is a British idiom for mad. Barmy is everyday British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: An army is a military force, the body of troops a nation fields.

clue.text: TV images on which cricket scores?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the patterned still pictures broadcast when no programme is on
second meaning, playful: the score sheets of a five-day international cricket match

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves split the answer differently: one is a broadcasting term, the other reads it as cards from an international match. A test is a cricket international.
explanation.definitionFit: Test cards were fixed images shown by broadcasters to calibrate sets, and the question mark admits the cricket score sheets are a playful second reading.

clue.text: Levy on fat cats?

parts.note: surface reading: a charge on overpaid bosses, the fat cats of business
setter's reading: a corporation is also a jocular word for a big belly, so a tax on the paunchy

explanation.walkthrough: The obvious fat cats are rich executives; the joke is that a corporation is also slang for a pot belly, so the levy falls on the fat.
explanation.definitionFit: The real tax is charged on company profits, and companies and their wealthy bosses are what fat cats suggests.

clue.text: Smoke, wasting a new bit of a joint

indicators.note: wasting something means losing it, so those letters drop out

parts.note: a panatella is a long, thin cigar
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone smokes a joint and wastes a fresh bit of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' tempts one to think of cannabis after 'Smoke', but it is the knee.
explanation.definitionFit: The patella is the kneecap, the small bone at the front of the knee joint.

clue.text: Plant's response requires replacing imports

indicators.note: replacing here means putting back in different places, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A factory's answer to supply problems is to switch to different imported goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a factory, which suits imports, but it is the green kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropism is a plant's growth movement towards or away from a stimulus such as light.

clue.text: Players' pitch

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the actors in a play, taken together
second meaning: to throw or fling

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a sports ground or a sales talk belonging to some players; instead the two words are separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names the company of actors in a production, and the verb means to throw, just as pitch does.

clue.text: Enough taste to dispense with starter

indicators.note: dispensing with the starter means dropping the first course, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: to taste is to sample

explanation.surface: A diner has had enough of the tasting menu and skips the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' looks like a first course, which suits taste; it means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means plentiful or more than sufficient, so it serves as enough.

clue.text: English firm maintained by pretty awful print worker

indicators.note: maintained by means held up and supported within, so the first pieces sit inside
something awful is a mess, so the word before it is jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English
set means firm, as a jelly that has set

explanation.surface: An English company is kept going by a really dreadful printer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company, beside 'English', but it is the adjective meaning solid. 'Pretty awful' reads as 'quite bad'; pretty is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A typesetter arranges type or text for printing, so is a worker in the print trade.

clue.text: Fair maiden in old novel held unfeeling in embrace of dish

indicators.note: the jumbled letters hold the next word, which sits inside them
to be in the embrace of something is to be wrapped inside it

parts.note: a plate is a dish

indicators.note: novel means new and fresh, so the two words before it take a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
numb means without feeling
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fair heroine in a classic novel is held by a cold-hearted villain, the stuff of old romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old novel' reads as a book from the past, but novel tells you to rearrange 'in old', which then holds unfeeling, all inside the dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A platinum blonde is a woman with very pale, silvery fair hair; fair here means light-haired, and maiden a young woman.

clue.text: Given some wires, I merely turned screw

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so the run is read from right to left
only some of the letters of the following words are wanted, a run sitting inside them

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the end of wires, the I and the start of merely

explanation.surface: An electrician confesses that, handed a few wires, they did nothing more than tighten a screw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screw' looks like part of the electrician's job but is the definition: in old slang a screw is a stingy person.
explanation.definitionFit: Screw is dated British slang for a skinflint who hoards money, the same as a miser.

clue.text: So long since it changed with old pope

indicators.note: letters that have changed have been moved into a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone muses that it has been ages since a change came with the election of an elderly pope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So long since' reads as one phrase about time passing, but the definition is 'So long' as a farewell. TOODLE-PIP is a jaunty, old-fashioned British way of saying goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: So long is an informal farewell, and toodle-pip is a breezy British equivalent of goodbye.

clue.text: Might her work involve correcting short solecisms?

definitions.text: Might her work involve correcting short solecisms?

parts.words: Might her work involve correcting short solecisms?
parts.note: surface reading: a woman whose job is fixing brief grammatical slips, like an editor
setter's reading: the errors are those made by short people, that is, children in a classroom

explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' seems to describe the mistakes as brief; it really describes the people making them, small pupils whose slips in grammar and manners a teacher puts right.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman teacher in a school spends much of her day correcting the grammatical and social blunders of young children.

clue.text: A talk about tiny boy — it's potentially explosive

definitions.note: read as 'something potentially explosive', a noun

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: about means around, so the chat goes round the boy

parts.note: to natter is to chatter idly
Tiny Tim is the crippled boy in Dickens's A Christmas Carol

explanation.surface: A heart-to-heart about a small boy could easily blow up into a row.
explanation.walkthrough: Natter is British informal for a chat. 'Potentially explosive' suggests a touchy conversation, but it is literal physics.
explanation.definitionFit: Antimatter annihilates on contact with ordinary matter in a burst of energy, making it a potential explosive.

clue.text: Dope clutching one translation of Bible in state of euphoria

indicators.note: to clutch something is to hold it tightly, so one word is held inside the other

parts.note: a nana is a silly fool, a dope
Roman numeral one
RV is the Revised Version, an English translation of the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone high on drugs clutches a Bible and feels blissfully transported.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' suggests drugs, which suits the euphoria, but here it is a fool. Nana is informal British for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Nirvana, the Buddhist state of release, is used loosely for any state of perfect bliss or elation.

clue.text: Sister hides hospital in jungle in which one wanted to be found?

definitions.text: in which one wanted to be found?

indicators.note: a thing that hides another keeps it out of sight inside itself

parts.note: a mat is a dense tangle, as of matted growth

indicators.note: one part is placed within the other word that follows

parts.note: a sister is a member of a religious order
H is the map symbol for a hospital

explanation.surface: A nursing sister hides a field hospital in the jungle, where someone is hoping to be rescued.
explanation.walkthrough: Hospital goes inside the sister, and that combination sits inside the tangled jungle. The definition's question mark flags its wordplay on 'wanted'.
explanation.definitionFit: A manhunt is an organised search for a person, typically a fugitive the police want, so the wanted one is meant to be found.

clue.text: Marriage needs to raise standard

parts.note: a marriage is a union
to jack up is to raise, as with a car jack

explanation.surface: A marriage needs both partners to lift their game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise standard' looks like improving quality, but standard is the definition, a flag.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a flag or banner, and the Union Jack is the national flag of the United Kingdom.

clue.text: At home, father holds power — move!

parts.note: someone at home is in

indicators.note: a word that holds another has it inside, between its own letters

parts.note: a sire is a father, especially of an animal
P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: A domineering father at home keeps all the authority and orders everyone else to shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Move!' looks like a shouted command; it is the definition in its sense of stirring someone's feelings.
explanation.definitionFit: To move someone emotionally or rouse them to act is to inspire them; the two verbs share that sense.

clue.text: Each girl virtually a pain

indicators.note: virtually means almost, so the name falls just short of complete

parts.note: EA is the abbreviation for each, as on price lists
Rachel is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Every girl is practically a nuisance, a grumble about difficult children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A pain' seems to call the girl annoying; it is the definition, a literal ache.
explanation.definitionFit: Earache is a pain in the ear, a common ailment.

clue.text: Cabinet member, one into crude stuff

parts.note: an arm is a limb, one of the body's members

indicators.note: going into something means being placed inside it

parts.note: ore is crude, unrefined material dug from the ground
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A government minister gets embroiled in something vulgar, a political scandal in a few words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cabinet member' reads as one phrase meaning a minister; split it, and the cabinet is the definition and the member is the limb.
explanation.definitionFit: An armoire is a large tall cupboard or wardrobe, a piece of furniture of the cabinet kind.

clue.text: One promising country's uprising ejects single ruler

indicators.note: in a down answer, rising up means the word reads from bottom to top
to eject something is to throw it out, so one letter is removed

parts.note: Russia is a country
I is the Roman numeral one, a single
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A revolutionary vows that the nation's revolt will throw out its sole autocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' looks like a revolt, fitting the political surface, but it turns the country upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: An assurer is a person who assures, giving a guarantee or promise that something is so.

clue.text: Tired with combat, sport?

parts.note: all in is informal for exhausted
wrestling is grappling hand to hand

explanation.surface: A soldier, weary of fighting, wonders whether the whole thing is a game.
explanation.walkthrough: All-in wrestling is a free-style form in which almost any hold is allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: All-in wrestling is a professional combat sport, a form of grappling with few banned holds.

clue.text: Shoot a beginner climbing in high city

indicators.note: climbing in a down clue means going upwards, so the letters read from the bottom

parts.note: to zap is to shoot, as with a ray gun
taken as written
L is a learner, as on L-plates

explanation.surface: A photographer shoots a novice mountaineer climbing in the Andes.
explanation.walkthrough: Shoot looks like photography or gunfire, and climbing like mountaineering; both point the wrong way.
explanation.definitionFit: La Paz in Bolivia sits about 3,600 metres above sea level, the highest seat of government in the world.

clue.text: God created height in prominence

indicators.note: one letter is put in, inside the word for the prominence

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, a prominence in the landscape
H is the abbreviation for height

explanation.surface: A creator deity raises a mountain out of flat land.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky outcrop, a word best known from Dartmoor in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Thor is the Norse god of thunder, wielder of the hammer.

clue.text: One trips on hard floor, and carpet rips

indicators.note: a ripped thing is torn apart, so these letters are pulled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles on a bare floor, and the rug tears as well: a small domestic accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trips' looks like stumbling, but it means stepping lightly, as in tripping the light fantastic, and the hard floor is where metal-tipped shoes make their noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A tap dancer steps nimbly over a hard surface so the metal plates on the shoes ring out.

clue.text: Under bovine, explosive gas

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle
H is the symbol for hydrogen, an explosive gas

explanation.surface: Beneath a cow lies a pocket of explosive gas, a farmyard hazard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under' seems to place the gas below the cow, but it is the definition; the pieces simply run in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Neath is a poetic shortening of beneath, so it means below or under.

clue.text: The thing won't begin level

indicators.note: something that will not begin is missing its start, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: a craze is whatever is all the rage, the thing everyone wants

explanation.surface: A stubborn machine refuses to start on a flat surface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The thing' seems to be an object that will not start, but it is the latest fashion, as in 'it's the thing'.
explanation.definitionFit: To raze a building is to level it, demolishing it completely to the ground.

clue.text: Direct without lead, without a right schmuck that's schmaltzy

definitions.note: read as a noun phrase: something that is schmaltzy

indicators.note: in its old sense of outside, so the shortened word goes round the following pieces
a word without its lead has lost its leading letter

parts.note: to steer is to direct or guide
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
a schmuck is a contemptible fool, a jerk

explanation.surface: A film director, leaderless, makes a mawkish weepie without some fool's input.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' appears twice: first it means lacking, then in its old sense of outside, wrapping the shortened verb round the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A tearjerker is a sentimental film or story designed to make audiences cry, exactly what schmaltz is.
